title: The storm and the tombs (Luke 8:22–39)
hook: he stills a storm, then heals a man living among graves
tomorrow: your faith has made you well

segments.voice: Yesterday: the sower and an honest and good heart, and your line, bear fruit with patience.

"Let us go over unto the other side of the lake." They push off, and he falls asleep in the boat. On a small boat, the mood can change in minutes. Luke says "there came down a storm of wind on the lake." Water pours in. Some of these men are fishermen who know this lake, and they're terrified. And the teacher is still asleep. Two stories follow, one on the water and one among graves, with a single thread: chaos, then a sudden quiet.
screen: `LET US GO OVER TO THE OTHER SIDE.`
`A STORM CAME DOWN ON THE LAKE.`

segments.voice: They wake him: "Master, master, we perish." And Luke says: "he arose, and rebuked the wind and the raging of the water: and they ceased, and there was a calm." The Greek for calm is galene, the glassy stillness of the sea after the wind drops. Then a question, not a lecture: "Where is your faith?" Now they're afraid in a new way, and full of wonder: "What manner of man is this! for he commandeth even the winds and water, and they obey him." On the far shore, in the country of the Gadarenes, pigs are feeding on the hillside. A man runs out who, Luke says, "ware no clothes, neither abode in any house, but in the tombs." Chained and guarded, he broke free again and again. Jesus asks a plain human question: "What is thy name?" He answers: "Legion." A legion was a Roman army unit, and Luke explains: "many devils were entered into him." He doesn't have a name of his own anymore, just a crowd. Jesus frees him; the spirits go into the pigs, which rush into the lake. The townspeople find the man "sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed, and in his right mind." The same quiet as on the lake. He begs to go with Jesus. Jesus says no: "Return to thine own house, and shew how great things God hath done unto thee." And he goes, telling the whole city.
screen: then, large: `RETURN TO THINE OWN HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Breathe slowly until the water inside you is a little glassier, then think of someone in a storm right now: a friend who's panicking, a child who can't sleep. You can't command the wind, but picture yourself as the calm one in the boat, a steady voice, a slow question: what's really going on? If you pray, you can hold them before God; if you don't, simply send them stillness.
Galene, the Greek word for a calm, the glassy stillness of the sea when the wind drops: Jesus stills a storm, then frees a man among the tombs and sends him home.

Your line: return to your house. A week of a centurion, a widow, John's question, a woman's tears, the women who paid, good soil and a calm sea. Day five hundred thirty-two, and another week on the path.

screen: `DAY 532 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: YOUR FAITH HAS MADE YOU WELL.`

howItsDone: Some Christians pray with the stilling of the storm in times of fear, and the healed man sent home to tell his story is sometimes read as a picture of faith shared first with family and neighbors.

what a scholar hears: "legion" was a Roman army word, and Luke explains it: many devils had entered him. the man ends the story sitting at Jesus' feet, clothed, in his right mind.

chat.meaning: Jesus said: return to thine own house, and shew how great things God hath done unto thee. He went and told the whole city.

galene.meaning: Greek for a calm, the sea gone glassy

Gadarenes.meaning: the people of the far shore, where the man lived

Legion.meaning: a Roman army unit; the man's name for himself
